title: Episode 138: James Buchanan and the Winter of Secession: The Star of the West
description:
Following the election of Abraham Lincoln on November sixth, eighteen sixty, the United States plunged into the darkest, most perilous winter of its existence. South Carolina immediately called a secession convention, and by February eighteen sixty-one, seven Deep South states had declared themselves separate from the United States, seizing federal arsenals, mints, custom houses, and forts across the South.

Sitting in the White House for four agonizing months before Lincoln's inauguration on March fourth was President James Buchanan. Paralyzed by legalistic pedantry and surrounded by treacherous Southern cabinet secretaries who were actively funneling federal arms to Southern militias, Buchanan delivered a bizarre, contradictory message to Congress: he declared that secession was illegal and unconstitutional, but that the federal government possessed no constitutional power to coerce a state or stop them!

When Major Robert Anderson moved his small federal garrison under cover of night to the island fortress of Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor, South Carolina demanded its immediate surrender. In January eighteen sixty-one, Buchanan dispatched an unarmed civilian merchant steamer, the Star of the West, with reinforcements and food for the starving garrison. When South Carolina shore batteries opened fire, the ship was hit and forced to retreat without firing a shot. Buchanan watched the nation crumble around him, counting the hours until he could flee the White House. Here is George with the tragic story of the Winter of Secession.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of President James Buchanan with the tragic collapse of the American Union during the winter of eighteen sixty and sixty-one. As state after state seceded and armed rebellion seized federal forts, President Buchanan sat in the White House paralyzed by legal doubts, refusing to act while his own cabinet conspired against him. Here is George with the story of the Winter of Secession and the Star of the West.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ELECTION THAT SHOOK THE WORLD
On the evening of Tuesday, November sixth, eighteen sixty, telegraph keys clicked in rapid, rhythmic succession across the United States. By midnight, the verdict was clear: Abraham Lincoln of Illinois, the candidate of the anti-slavery Republican Party, had been elected the sixteenth President of the United States. Lincoln had won an overwhelming majority in the Electoral College without carrying a single Southern state, winning not a single popular vote across most of the Deep South.
In Charleston, South Carolina, the news was greeted not with despair, but with wild, euphoric celebrations. Red cockades were pinned to lapels, fireworks lit the night sky, and military bands paraded through the streets playing the Marseillaise. For thirty years, Southern radicals had dreamed of an independent Southern confederacy, and Lincoln's election was the long-awaited catalyst. On December twentieth, eighteen sixty, a special convention meeting at St. Andrew's Hall in Charleston unanimously passed the Ordinance of Secession, dissolving the union between South Carolina and the other states of America.
Within six weeks, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas followed, passing ordinances of secession and establishing a provisional government at Montgomery, Alabama, electing Jefferson Davis as President of the Confederate States of America. But Abraham Lincoln would not take the oath of office until March fourth, eighteen sixty-one. For four long, agonizing months, the fate of the American republic rested in the trembling hands of a paralyzed, weeping bachelor in the White House: James Buchanan.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DOCTRINE OF PARALYSIS
On December third, eighteen sixty, President James Buchanan delivered his Fourth Annual Message to Congress. It was one of the most bizarre, intellectually bankrupt state papers in the history of human governance. Buchanan laid out a tortured, contradictory legal philosophy that left both the North and the South in bewildered disbelief.
First, Buchanan blamed the entire crisis on Northern abolitionists, declaring that the South was merely reacting in justified self-defense against Northern moral agitation over slavery. Second, Buchanan declared that secession was an unconstitutional, revolutionary act that destroyed the perpetual Union of the framers.
But then came Buchanan's fatal, paralyzing conclusion. He argued that while a state had no constitutional right to secede, the federal government had no constitutional power under the law to coerce a seceding state or use military force to preserve the Union. Buchanan asserted that the Constitution gave Congress the power to declare war against foreign nations, but not against a sovereign state of the American union.
The doctrine was suicidal nonsense. William H. Seward sarcastically summarized Buchanan's position to the Senate: 'The President shows conclusively that a state has no right to secede, unless it wants to; and that the federal government has the full power to enforce the laws, unless somebody resists them.' Buchanan had announced to the rebels that the United States government would not lift a hand to stop them.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: TREASON IN THE CABINET ROOM
While Buchanan wrung his hands in tearful indecision, treason was actively operating inside his own cabinet room. His Secretary of War, John B. Floyd of Virginia, used his executive authority to systematically transfer over one hundred and fifteen thousand muskets, rifles, and heavy cannons from federal armories in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania to federal arsenals in the Deep South, ensuring that Southern militias would be armed to the teeth when secession was declared.
His Secretary of the Treasury, Howell Cobb of Georgia, spent the autumn mismanaging the federal finances, driving the United States Treasury to the verge of bankruptcy before resigning to help organize the Confederate government. His Secretary of the Interior, Jacob Thompson of Mississippi, took an official leave of absence from the cabinet to travel to North Carolina as a secession commissioner, actively urging that state to leave the Union while remaining on the federal payroll.
State after state in the Deep South seized federal property without firing a shot. Confederate militias marched into federal custom houses, took over post offices, seized federal mints containing over half a million dollars in gold coin in New Orleans, and occupied dozens of coastal forts and arsenals. Buchanan looked on in helpless despair, afraid that any defensive military action by the federal government would provoke the border slave states—Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri—into joining the Confederacy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: MAJOR ANDERSON AT FORT SUMTER
In the midst of this humiliating collapse, one solitary American soldier took a stand for national honor. In Charleston harbor, Major Robert Anderson commanded a tiny federal garrison of eighty-five soldiers of the First United States Artillery, stationed at Fort Moultrie on the mainland. Fort Moultrie was indefensible against land assault, surrounded by drifting sand dunes that allowed Confederate snipers to fire directly into the fort's courtyard.
Out in the center of the harbor sat Fort Sumter—a massive, unfinished five-sided brick fortress with walls five feet thick rising fifty feet above the water, bristling with heavy cannon casemates. On the dark, moonless night of December twenty-sixth, eighteen sixty, Major Anderson made an audacious, unauthorized command decision. Spiking his guns at Fort Moultrie and burning the gun carriages, Anderson quietly evacuated his men, their families, and supplies into rowboats, rowing across the darkened harbor to occupy Fort Sumter.
At noon on December twenty-seventh, Anderson assembled his little garrison in the center of Fort Sumter's parade ground. Kneeling in prayer, Anderson hauled the thirty-three-star American flag to the top of the fortress flagpole while his men cheered. Across the North, news of Anderson's bold move ignited an electric wave of patriotic euphoria; church bells pealed, and Anderson was hailed as the first hero of the Union. But in Charleston and the White House, it detonated fury.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE STAR OF THE WEST
South Carolina authorities were beside themselves with rage, accusing Anderson of a treacherous breach of peace. South Carolina commissioners arrived in Washington, arrogantly demanding that President Buchanan immediately order Anderson to evacuate Fort Sumter and surrender the fortress to the state. When Buchanan wavered, his remaining Northern cabinet officers—new Attorney General Edwin M. Stanton and Secretary of State Jeremiah Black—threatened mass resignation, warning Buchanan that if he surrendered Fort Sumter, he would be guilty of treason and impeached.
Stung into action, Buchanan finally authorized a relief expedition. General Winfield Scott initially proposed sending the powerful naval warship USS Brooklyn with heavy cannons and two hundred regular soldiers. But Buchanan, terrified of provoking a battle, insisted on an unarmed, civilian vessel. On the night of January fifth, eighteen sixty-one, the unarmed civilian merchant paddle steamer Star of the West slipped out of New York harbor, carrying two hundred federal soldiers hidden below deck, along with ammunition and three months of food supplies.
At dawn on January ninth, eighteen sixty-one, the Star of the West steamed into the main ship channel of Charleston harbor, flying a massive American garrison flag. As she passed Morris Island, a battery of heavy artillery manned by teenage cadets from The Citadel opened fire. A cannonball whistled across the ship's bow, followed by heavy shellfire that struck the wooden hull. Looking on from Fort Sumter, Major Anderson's gunners manned their heavy coastal guns, begging for orders to return fire and blast the rebel batteries. But Anderson, lacking explicit authorization from Washington and fearing the destruction of the unarmed steamer, held his fire. Battered by shells and lacking naval escorts, the Star of the West turned around and retreated to New York. The first shots of the Civil War had been fired, and the United States government had retreated in humiliation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: COUNTING THE DAYS TO DELIVERANCE
Following the humiliation of the Star of the West, James Buchanan surrendered all initiative. He entered into an informal, humiliating truce with South Carolina authorities: the rebels agreed not to attack Fort Sumter, provided Buchanan sent no further reinforcements or supplies. Major Anderson and his eighty-five men were left isolated on their brick island, eating diminishing rations of salted pork and hardtack, surrounded by miles of Confederate earthworks and heavy siege mortars.
In the Executive Mansion, Buchanan became a phantom president. He spent his days sitting by the window in his study, looking haggard, pale, and trembling with nervous exhaustion. He received hundreds of pieces of hate mail every day, including crude drawings of nooses and coffins. When friends visited, they found the President pacing the floor in tears, praying aloud that God would preserve the peace until his term expired.
Buchanan was obsessed with one thing alone: running out the clock. He wanted to avoid a shooting war at all costs during his administration, desperate to hand the catastrophic nightmare over to Abraham Lincoln so that history would blame his successor for the bloodshed. On Capitol Hill, compromise efforts like the Crittenden Compromise collapsed, while in Texas, General David Twiggs committed the ultimate treason, surrendering all federal military posts in the state—and over one million dollars in military supplies—to Confederate authorities without firing a shot.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RIDE TO THE INAUGURATION
Finally, on the morning of Monday, March fourth, eighteen sixty-one, the nightmare came to an end. At noon, an open carriage pulled up to the north portico of the White House. James Buchanan, dressed in his formal black broadcloth suit, stepped inside alongside the President-elect, Abraham Lincoln.
Surrounded by heavy cavalry escorts and riflemen positioned on rooftops by General Winfield Scott to prevent Confederate assassination attempts, the two men rode down Pennsylvania Avenue toward the Capitol. Buchanan looked exhausted, withered, and ancient, while the towering, sixty-one-year-old Lincoln sat erect, his rugged face etched with solemn, unyielding resolve.
As the carriage rolled along the dusty avenue, Buchanan turned to Lincoln, looked him in the eye, and whispered one of the most famous, poignant lines in American history: 'My dear sir, if you are as happy in entering the White House as I shall feel on returning to Wheatland, you are a happy man indeed.' Lincoln replied with quiet gravity: 'Mr. President, I shall endeavor to do my duty.'
Hours later, after witnessing Lincoln deliver his First Inaugural Address—pleading with the South by appealing to the 'mystic chords of memory'—James Buchanan boarded a train at the Washington depot and departed the capital forever. Behind him, the American Union was in ashes. Five weeks later, Confederate cannons opened fire on Fort Sumter, plunging the nation into four years of bloody civil war that would claim seven hundred and fifty thousand American lives.
James Buchanan spent his remaining years secluded at Wheatland, writing defensive memoirs attempting to justify his actions, universally condemned by historians as the worst president in American history. He proved to posterity that when the foundations of a great republic are under attack, cowardice, indecision, and legal pedantry are not neutrality—they are the handmaidens of national ruin.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
James Buchanan's paralysis during the Winter of Secession left the American Union shattered and on the brink of destruction. Next week, we turn to the savior of the republic, America's sixteenth President, Abraham Lincoln, and the pivotal moment in February eighteen sixty when he arrived in New York City to deliver the Cooper Union speech—proclaiming that 'right makes might' and setting off on the improbable journey that would save American democracy. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
